incoming.name: Lawn
incoming.excerpt: For example, in the New Forest, England, such grazed areas still occur commonly and are still called lawns, for example Balmer Lawn.

incoming.name: William II of England
incoming.section: The unusual death of William II
incoming.excerpt: Perhaps the most memorable event in the life of William Rufus was his death, which occurred while William was hunting in the New Forest.

outgoing.name: Bronze Age
outgoing.excerpt: Like much of England, the New Forest was originally forested, but parts were cleared for cultivation from the Stone Age and into the Bronze Age.

outgoing.name: Domesday Book
outgoing.excerpt: It was first recorded as "Nova Foresta" in the Domesday Book in 1086.

outgoing.name: European Union
outgoing.excerpt: The New Forest is designated as an EU Special Area of Conservation.

outgoing.name: Great Britain
outgoing.excerpt: The area contains a profusion of rare wildlife, including the New Forest cicada, the only cicada native to Great Britain.

outgoing.name: Royal Navy
outgoing.excerpt: Over time, the New Forest became an important source of wood for the Royal Navy, and plantations were begun to replace the felled trees.

outgoing.name: Stone Age
outgoing.excerpt: Like much of England, the New Forest was originally forested, but parts were cleared for cultivation from the Stone Age and into the Bronze Age.

outgoing.name: William I of England
outgoing.excerpt: The New Forest was created as a royal forest in 1079 by William the Conqueror for the hunting of (mainly) deer.

outgoing.name: William II of England
outgoing.excerpt: William's successor, William Rufus was killed in a suspicious accident while hunting in the New Forest in 1100.

outgoing.name: World Heritage Site
outgoing.excerpt: The New Forest was proposed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in June 1999, and it became a National Park in 2005.
